lead: A shaft can pass the strength check and still fail in service. If it bends too far, gear teeth mesh badly and bearings wear at one edge. If it spins near its lateral natural frequency, a tiny unbalance grows into violent whirl. So a shaft needs two more checks: rigidity, meaning limits on deflection and slope, and critical speed, the spin speed where whirl peaks. Pump shafts, turbine rotors and the motor shaft of a workshop blower all get this check before the drawing is released.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.1 for shaft loading and combined stress, and Unit 1 for beam deflection by double integration and Macaulay's method.

blocks.text: Chapter 3.1 fixes the diameter from combined bending and torsion stress. The same diameter must also be stiff enough. Stiffness depends on the product EI, and I grows as d⁴, so doubling the diameter cuts deflection to one-sixteenth. A shaft that is strong enough can still be too flexible.
Two quantities are limited. Deflection y is the sideways movement in metres, checked at the gear or the rotor. Slope θ = dy/dx is in radians, checked at the bearings and at the gear mesh.

items: Slope at a bearing tilts the inner ring on the shaft, so the rolling elements load one edge and bearing life drops.
Slope at a gear mesh tilts the teeth against each other, contact moves to the tooth ends, and noise and pitting follow.
Deflection between gears changes the centre distance and the backlash; deflection at a seal changes the clearance, which can rub on one side.

blocks.text: Design offices commonly allow a slope of about 0.001 rad at a bearing and a deflection of a few hundredths to about a tenth of a millimetre at a gear mesh. Your design code fixes the exact number; the worked example uses 0.08 mm.

blocks.where: δ is the midspan deflection in metres; W is the load at midspan in newtons; L is the span between bearings in metres; E is Young's modulus in N/m²; I is the second moment of area of the section in m⁴.

blocks.text: That formula assumes a uniform simply supported shaft with one central load. Real shafts are stepped, so I changes from span to span and Macaulay's method from Unit 1 is the hand tool.

items: Draw the free body and find the bearing reactions; gear and pulley forces come from Unit 7.
Write one bending moment equation M(x) for the whole length, using Macaulay brackets so each load starts acting only after its own position.
Integrate twice with the correct I for each span: E I y″ = M(x), then E I y′ = ∫M dx + C₁ and E I y = ∫∫M dx dx + C₁x + C₂.
Apply y = 0 at both bearings and continuity of y and slope at every step, solve for the constants, and read y at the rotor and y′ at the bearings.

blocks.text: A shaft with three or four diameters takes about half a page of hand algebra. A spreadsheet or a beam element code does the same in seconds and is the normal route in industry.

No rotor is perfectly balanced. Its centre of mass lies a small distance e from the shaft's geometric centre. At spin speed ω rad/s the centre of mass is at radius y + e from the rotation axis, so the centrifugal force is m(y + e)ω². The bent shaft pushes back with k y, where k is the lateral stiffness in N/m and y is the whirl amplitude in metres. Equating forces gives the undamped whirl amplitude y = e r²/(1 − r²), where r = ω/ω<sub>n</sub> and ω<sub>n</sub> = √(k/m) is the lateral natural frequency in rad/s. With damping ratio ζ, y = e r²/√((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²). As r reaches 1 the amplitude peaks. At high speed r ≫ 1 the shaft rotates about its centre of mass and the magnitude of y tends to e.

Damping keeps the peak finite, but a shaft run at its critical speed still shakes hard enough to wipe a bearing in minutes. Keep the running speed at least about 25 % away from N<sub>c</sub>, or pass through it quickly while starting.
For a simply supported shaft with the rotor at midspan, k = 48EI/L³ and the static deflection is δ = W/k, so k/m = g/δ.

blocks.where: N_c is the first critical speed in rpm; δ is the static deflection at the rotor in metres; g = 9.81 m/s²; the factor 60/2π = 9.5493 converts rad/s to rpm.

blocks.text: A rotor that sags 1 mm has N<sub>c</sub> near 946 rpm; at 0.07 mm it is about 3575 rpm. Halving δ raises N<sub>c</sub> by √2, so a small gain in stiffness buys a large gain in speed.

Rayleigh's method handles several masses. Guess a deflection shape y(x), for example by loading the shaft with all the weights at once, read y<sub>i</sub> at each mass, and compute ω<sub>n</sub> = √(g ΣW<sub>i</sub> y<sub>i</sub> / ΣW<sub>i</sub> y<sub>i</sub>²), with W<sub>i</sub> in newtons and y<sub>i</sub> in metres. The guess gives a frequency slightly above the true one.

Dunkerley's method adds the separate effects: 1/N<sub>c</sub>² ≈ 1/N₁² + 1/N₂² + …, where N<sub>i</sub> is the critical speed with mass i alone. It gives a value slightly below the true one. Only a few universities teach it.

Critical speed here is lateral: it comes from bending stiffness EI and the mass. A shaft also has torsional natural frequencies, set by the torsional stiffness GJ and the polar mass moment of inertia; a torsional resonance twists the shaft with no sideways movement. These are different numbers and are checked separately.

figure.caption: Whirl amplitude divided by eccentricity against speed ratio r = ω/ω_n for a damping ratio of 0.15. The amplitude starts at zero, peaks near r = 1, the critical speed, and tends to the eccentricity e at high speed.

spec.aria: Plot of shaft whirl amplitude divided by eccentricity against speed ratio, starting at zero, peaking at the critical speed ratio of one, and tending to one at high speed.

examples.question: A steel shaft of diameter 60 mm and span 1.2 m between bearings carries a rotor of mass 25 kg at midspan. Take E = 200 GPa and g = 9.81 m/s². Find the static deflection at midspan and the first critical speed, and state whether the deflection is below the permitted 0.08 mm. Neglect the shaft's own mass.
steps: Second moment of area: I = πd⁴/64 = π(0.060 m)⁴/64 = 6.362 × 10⁻⁷ m⁴.
Rotor weight: W = m g = 25 kg × 9.81 m/s² = 245.25 N.
Check: 0.0694 mm < 0.08 mm, so the deflection is within the permitted limit.
The shaft's own mass is neglected; counting it would add to δ and lower N_c slightly.
examples.answer: Static deflection is 0.0694 mm, below the 0.08 mm limit, and the first critical speed is about 3590 rpm; the running speed must stay at least about 25 % away from it.
examples.check:
import math
d = 0.060
L = 1.2
m = 25.0
E = 200e9
g = 9.81
I = math.pi*d**4/64
W = m*g
delta = W*L**3/(48*E*I)
Nc = 60/(2*math.pi)*math.sqrt(g/delta)
print(round(W, 2))
print(round(delta*1000, 4))
print(round(Nc, 1))

traps: Putting δ in millimetres into N_c = (60/2π)√(g/δ) while g is in m/s² makes the answer √1000 ≈ 31.6 times too small. Convert δ to metres first.
ω_n = √(g/δ) is in rad/s. Multiply by 60/(2π) to get rpm; skipping that step is a standard mark loss.
Critical speed is a speed, not a stress limit. The answer must end in rpm, and a shaft can be strong and still whirl.
δ = W L³/(48 E I) holds only for a central load on a simply supported span. For the shaft's own weight as a uniformly distributed load w, use δ = 5wL⁴/(384 E I).
Lateral critical speed (bending, E and I) is not torsional resonance (twisting, G and J). Read which one the question asks.

quiz.q: Define the critical speed of a shaft and give its unit.
quiz.a: The spin speed at which the rotational frequency equals the natural frequency of lateral vibration, so whirl amplitude peaks. It is measured in rpm (or rad/s).

quiz.q: Why can a shaft that passes the strength check still be rejected at the design stage?
quiz.a: Strength checks stress only. A slender shaft may have low stress but excessive deflection and slope at gears and bearings, and a low critical speed, so it fails on rigidity and whirl.

quiz.q: Write the formula for the first critical speed of a simply supported shaft with a central mass and state the unit of δ.
quiz.a: N_c = (60/2π)√(g/δ), with δ the static deflection at the rotor in metres, g = 9.81 m/s², and N_c in rpm.

quiz.q: A simply supported shaft has a static deflection of 0.25 mm at the rotor. Find its first critical speed.
A shaft runs steadily at 1440 rpm and its static deflection is 0.30 mm. Comment on safety and suggest one change.
quiz.a: δ = 3 × 10⁻⁴ m gives N_c = 9.5493 × √(9.81/3 × 10⁻⁴) = 1727 rpm. The running speed 0.83 N_c is inside the 25 % band, so whirl will be severe. Increase the diameter (I rises as d⁴), shorten the span, or add a bearing near the rotor to raise N_c.

quiz.q: What happens to whirl amplitude above the critical speed?
quiz.a: Above critical speed the shaft rotates about its centre of mass. The whirl amplitude tends to the eccentricity e; it does not fall to zero. The deflection remains about e, small only because e is small, so bearing forces are small and the shaft runs smoothly.

beyond: Not for the exam. Large turbomachinery is checked with full rotor dynamics software that adds gyroscopic stiffening, oil-film bearing stiffness and damping, and computes a Campbell diagram of natural frequency against speed. Passing through a critical speed during run-up is routine in steam turbines and is handled by rapid acceleration. Standards such as API 617 set how many lateral and torsional modes must be shown clear of the operating speed. Search terms to start with: rotor dynamics, Campbell diagram, Dunkerley's method, API 617 lateral analysis.
